body.text: Attribution: Shairee Malhotra, “EU-India SDP: Opportunities and Limits for Defence Industrial Cooperation,” ORF Issue Brief No. 907, Observer Research Foundation, November 2026.

In January 2026, India and the European Union (EU) signed a Security and Defence Partnership (SDP)[1] at the 16th EU-India Summit[2] in New Delhi. Although public attention largely centred on the conclusion of the long-awaited EU–India Free Trade Agreement (FTA), the SDP represents a milestone. For the first time, Brussels and New Delhi established a comprehensive framework dedicated to security and defence cooperation, signalling that the relationship has evolved beyond its historical focus on economic ties. The SDP institutionalises cooperation across a broad spectrum of domains, including maritime security, defence industry, cyber and hybrid threats, counterterrorism, space, emerging technologies, and organised crime.[3]

The agreement fits within the EU's broader strategic approach to security partnerships. Since the adoption of the Strategic Compass in 2022,[a],[4] SDPs have become pillars of the Union’s foreign and security policy. They are designed as frameworks of cooperation aimed at strengthening the EU’s bilateral relations with like-minded non-EU countries. The EU has signed 12 SDPs so far;[5] the EU-India SDP, however, differs from many of these. The SDPs with NATO allies Norway, the United Kingdom (UK), and Canada build on pre-existing security ties. Those with the enlargement countries Albania, Moldova, and North Macedonia aim to counter Russian influence. The SDP with Ghana focuses on counterterrorism and capacity building in West Africa.

The EU-India SDP, for its part, belongs to a category of partnerships with key Indo-Pacific partners such as Japan, South Korea, and Australia. These partnerships are aimed at enhancing stability in the Indo-Pacific region and contributing to a more resilient global security architecture. This is done by, among others, promoting defence-industrial cooperation and capability development.[6]
This brief explores the rationale behind the EU-India SDP and assesses the scope for closer defence industrial ties. It outlines recommendations for measures to advance cooperation.
The EU-India SDP has come at a time when the global security environment is rapidly deteriorating and both Europe and India are reassessing their strategic priorities.

For Europe, Russia’s war on Ukraine, ongoing now for nearly five years, has transformed its security outlook and accelerated the EU’s emergence as a geopolitical actor. At the same time, uncertainty over American security guarantees under President Donald Trump’s second term has raised European concerns about long-term strategic dependence on the United States (US). Washington’s increasingly transactional approach towards NATO, including pressure on allies to raise defence spending to 5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), has reinforced Europe’s quest for greater strategic autonomy.[7] EU-China relations, meanwhile, continue to be strained by Chinese economic coercion, industrial overcapacity, and Beijing’s support for Russia.[8]

For India, Trump’s punitive tariffs, Washington’s evolving engagement with Pakistan, and other frictions, have served as a reality check on India-US relations, once described as “the defining partnership of the 21st century.”[9] In addition, the role played by Chinese arms supplies to Pakistan during Operation Sindoor in May 2025, underscored the robust strategic convergence between Beijing and Islamabad. These developments confirmed the China-Pakistan axis as India’s principal security challenge, and also highlighted the intertwined nature of the Indo-Pacific and Euro-Atlantic theatres when it comes to security, energy, and trade flows.[10]

Four structural shocks have strengthened the case for a closer EU-India security partnership: Russia’s war on Ukraine; China’s assertiveness and expansionism in the Indo-Pacific; eroding trust in the US; and tensions between India and Pakistan. While their threat perceptions are not identical, the EU and India converge on issues such as maritime security, maintaining a free and open Indo-Pacific, de-risking dependencies in critical sectors, and the need for military procurement diversification away from traditional suppliers, namely the US and Russia.[11]

Only five years ago, former EU Ambassador to India Hervé Delphin has noted, the SDP would not have been conceivable.[12] With security in the Indo-Pacific and Euro-Atlantic theatres intertwined through supply chains, defence technologies, and wider strategic competition, New Delhi and Brussels have recognised the need to strengthen cooperation. Against this backdrop, the EU-India SDP reflects shared ambitions amidst broader geopolitical shifts and disruptions.

The EU’s SDPs are non-legally binding instruments. Instead of obligatory security guarantees, they prioritise frameworks, dialogues, and institutional mechanisms to cooperate in areas of shared interest. This sits well with India’s aversion to traditional alliances and preference for policy flexibility. Each SDP is tailored to the partner country and contains a review clause for adjustments.

The EU-India SDP has the potential to transform defence-industrial cooperation from a collection of bilateral initiatives into a more structured, long-term strategic partnership, moving beyond a typical buyer-seller model. It arrives at a pivotal moment, as Europe undertakes its most significant rearmament effort yet,[13] while India seeks to consolidate years of defence reforms into its emergence as a defence manufacturing and export hub.[14] Together, these trends create an unprecedented opportunity to integrate the European and Indian defence-industrial ecosystems.

The new EU-India Strategic Agenda recognises that Europe’s security will depend on strengthening its own defence capabilities, and also on building partnerships with trusted countries.[15] The agenda reinforces this direction through consultations on defence initiatives and industrial cooperation. The SDP commits to exploring India’s participation “in relevant EU defence initiatives.”[16] While any participation will remain subject to legal frameworks and political approval, the SDP marks the first formal possibility that India could become part of Europe’s evolving defence architecture.

The SDP offers mechanisms for translating political convergence into practical cooperation. These include an annual Security and Defence Dialogue, a dedicated EU-India Defence Industry Forum, and negotiations towards a Security of Information Agreement (SoIA), which is a prerequisite for “more sensitive” security cooperation.

An industrial opportunity lies in the potential for India to access the EU’s Security Action for Europe (SAFE) instrument. Introduced in 2025, SAFE offers loans worth 150 billion euro to expand defence production, joint procurement, and industrial capacity across the EU.[17] It is part of the Union’s broader ReArm Europe initiative, worth 800 billion euro, designed to strengthen European defence and industrial capabilities.[18] Access to SAFE could allow Indian firms to contribute to joint procurement programmes, co-production, and capability development.

As noted earlier, these pressures are pushing European governments to expand production capacity and diversify defence partnerships. However, defence production continues to be a constraint when it comes to European military readiness. As acknowledged in the European Defence Industrial Strategy released in 2024, the sector is characterised by chronic underinvestment, fragmented production lines, and short-term procurement cycles.[19] SAFE is an EU response to these challenges.

Meanwhile, India’s defence needs remain acute, with a pressing need to bolster and modernise military capabilities. Although India renewed a 10-year defence pact with the US,[20] the trust deficit between the two persists,[21] accelerating New Delhi’s desire to expand its pool of defence partners beyond Washington and Moscow. Delays in the General Electric (GE)-Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) F414 fighter engine programme, and a downgrading of the Quad,[22] have raised concerns about Washington’s reliability as a security partner.

According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), Russia’s share of India’s defence imports declined from 69 percent in 2012-2016 to 36 percent in 2019-2023.[23] Russia’s preoccupation with the war in Ukraine and its own defence needs have resulted in delays in deliveries of critical platforms to India, such as the S-400 air defence system and Admiral Grigorovich-class frigates.[24] Moscow’s growing dependence on Beijing for components, including those used in the S-400, coupled with sanctions and production bottlenecks, have compounded Indian concerns of over-reliance on a few external suppliers.[25],[26],[27] Against this backdrop, European suppliers are being viewed as reliable alternatives.

India already has robust bilateral defence relations with several EU member states, spanning various defence platforms and joint production. Key examples include the Scorpène submarines that India is building with French technology, the collaboration between Airbus Spain and Tata Advanced Systems (TASL) to manufacture C-295 aircraft in Gujarat, and Italy’s Leonardo partnership with Adani Defence and Aerospace on helicopter production. Indeed, France remains India’s most trusted defence partner in Europe. Companies such as Safran have established industrial partnerships with Indian firms, with approvals to purchase 114 more Rafale fighter jets in addition to 26 Rafale marine carrier-based variants.[28]

At the same time, Germany’s ThyssenKrupp Marine Systems (TKMS) and India’s Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders are building six advanced diesel-electric submarines with air-independent propulsion to bolster India’s naval capabilities.[29] The deal may include some level of technology transfer in submarine production, which is typically a very closely guarded domain. TKMS also has long-term ambitions to convert India into a submarine-manufacturing hub and cater to third-country markets.[30] India may benefit from closer ties with Poland, which is increasingly becoming a world leader in drone warfare and defence innovation.[31] Sweden’s Saab, meanwhile, is co-producing the Carl-Gustaf M4 weapon system in Haryana.[32]

Several of these bilateral projects are structured around co-development, localisation of production, and technology sharing rather than direct exports. Indian procurement is now firmly anchored to domestic production and capability building. The SDP provides an opportunity to complement and reinforce, rather than replace, these bilateral relationships within an overarching EU framework.

Yet, defence industrial operation is no longer one-way. Indian firms are also increasingly supplying to Europe, to replenish stockpiles depleted by the Ukraine war and address critical shortages. India has developed competitive strengths that align with European requirements in ammunition, loitering munitions, drones, missiles, artillery systems and components, most of which are priority areas identified in the EU White Paper for European Defence Readiness 2030.[33] Indian defence exports to Europe have expanded from US$2.8 million before the Russia-Ukraine war to US$67.4 million in 2023–24 and US$135.6 million during the first nine months of FY2024–25.[34] Indian-manufactured 155 mm artillery shells cost much less than Western alternatives, resulting in a US$68-million export order for artillery shells from German firm Rheinmetall to Reliance Defence.[35] Rafale cooperation now includes “sustainment, engines, long-term maintenance ecosystems,”[36] which Europe itself needs.

India is well-positioned to fit in Europe’s rearmament ambitions given its capacity to scale, lower production costs, a large and skilled low-cost workforce, and a fast-developing defence industrial ecosystem spanning unmanned systems, components, electronics, aerospace, shipbuilding, maintenance infrastructure, supported by government initiatives such as Make in India and Atmanirbhar Bharat. As Indian Defence Minister Rajnath Singh stated as the SDP was signed, “Indian defence industry can play a meaningful role in the EU’s ReArm initiative.”[37]

India, however, lacks access to advanced technologies, and a 2024 report estimates that “Indian defence firms have a research and development (R&D) intensity of 1.2 percent, compared to 3.4 percent among global defence firms.”[38] While Europe is unable to match India’s cost and labour efficiency and scale, it is a global leader in defence R&D and advanced military technologies that can support India’s defence industrial base and integration into more advanced value chains through co-development and potential technology access.

The EU-India partnership aligns with India’s broader goals for indigenous defence manufacturing and export. Domestic defence production has reached record levels, and exports dramatically expanded over the last decade. By 2029, India aims to boost defence export targets to US$5.8 billion from US$2.8 billion in 2025, a 34-fold increase since 2013-14, and production targets to around US$34.7 billion by 2029 from US$ 17.4 billion in FY 2024-25.[39] India’s 2026-27 defence budget is approximately US$90.8 billion, amounting to 2 percent of GDP.[40] Greater integration with European defence supply chains may increase production and exports while providing potential access to advanced technologies, foreign investment, and high-value manufacturing opportunities. In doing so, it could strengthen industrial autonomy rather than simply filling capability gaps.[41]

The conclusion of the EU-India FTA may also facilitate EU-India defence cooperation, as highlighted by Andrius Kubilius, European Commissioner for Defence and Space.[42] Although the FTA is intended to strengthen trade, investment, and civil industrial collaboration, defence planners see it as a foundation for expanding defence cooperation, acquiring military equipment, and building resilient supply chains.[43]

Beyond industrial benefits, the SDP carries wider strategic significance, particularly in the Indo-Pacific region, where Europe has struggled to expand its footprint.[44] The SDP may embed Europe more firmly within the Indo-Pacific region through maritime security cooperation and integration into defence supply chains. Both India and Europe seek to enhance deterrence and capabilities in the Indo-Pacific, and shape the balance of power in the region.

A fundamental divergence lies in differing threat perceptions. Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, the EU has viewed Moscow as an existential security threat. India, in contrast, sees China as its long-term security challenge, driven by unresolved border disputes, Beijing’s expanding maritime footprint, and the growing China-Pakistan nexus. While New Delhi has steadily diversified its defence imports, Moscow remains a key partner, particularly in maintenance and legacy platforms, where over 60-70 percent of India’s inventory is of Russian or Soviet origin.[45]

India is also watching how Europe’s China policy unfolds. Although Brussels has pledged to ‘de-risk’ from China, EU member states continue to maintain substantial economic ties with Beijing.[46] From New Delhi’s perspective, Europe's equidistant response to the 2020 Galwan clashes[47] and its continued engagement with Pakistan, including preferential market access under the GSP+ scheme despite India's long-standing terrorism concerns,[48] raise questions about the extent of EU-India strategic convergence. The India-Poland diplomatic spat in January 2026 over Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski’s visit to Pakistan in October 2025,[49] and India’s participation in the Zapad military exercises with Russia and Belarus further illustrate differences.[50] These differences may prevent deeper security cooperation and instead limit it to low-hanging fruits such as humanitarian relief or anti-piracy operations.

For European firms, intellectual property protection and the potential leakage of sensitive technologies is a concern. The proposed SoIA would provide for exchanging classified information, and potentially high-end technology transfers, subject to member-state approval and export-control regimes. Security concerns resulting from divergent threat perceptions and a lack of strategic trust, however, may render difficulties in negotiating terms for technology transfers and other issues.

Regulatory frameworks present another obstacle. Both sides are pursuing greater defence self-reliance by prioritising domestic procurement. SAFE requires at least 65 percent of the component costs of jointly financed defence systems to originate within the EU, Ukraine, or the European Economic Area (EEA), limiting non-EU participation to 35 percent.[51] India’s Defence Acquisition Procedure (DAP 2020) similarly prioritises indigenous manufacturing. Categories such as Buy Indian-IDDM, or Indigenously Designed, Developed and Manufactured, require at least 50 percent indigenous content.[52] Bridging these competing production localisation thresholds is difficult, and simultaneously undermines the economic rationale for co-production.

While the SDP provides the first prerequisite for future Indian participation in SAFE, a subsequent bilateral agreement is required before India can obtain financing. This may be a long shot. So far, Canada is only the third country with access to SAFE. Even the UK has been unable to join.[53] The EU may consider making its frameworks less rigid and better suited for third-country participation that benefits both sides.

The fragmentation of the European defence industry and competition between member states are further issues. The EU attempts to strengthen a common European defence portfolio, an effort made complicated by different export controls and licensing regimes.

India and Europe still rely largely on government-to-government procurement defence deals centred on major platforms. While useful, this model is too slow for fast-moving technologies and fails to foster deep industrial integration. Critical design, intellectual property, and high-value technologies remain concentrated with European firms, leaving Indian companies largely in component manufacturing, assembly, or support roles.[54]

Finally, trade is an EU competence, but security and defence decision-making primarily remains a national one, potentially limiting progress and deliverables at the EU level. The EU-India security and defence cooperation is therefore likely to remain anchored in bilateral ties. Moreover, strengthening defence-industrial cooperation with the EU could create challenges for India’s bilateral defence ties with individual member states if those relationships become increasingly governed by EU-wide rules and standardised procedures for defence procurement.

Divergences over fundamental threat perceptions will remain, requiring pragmatic accommodation rather than pressure. The Russia factor, however, has not been a fault-line in deepening EU-India relations. The decision to conclude the SDP suggests that “shared issue-based interests outweigh full ideological alignment as a criterion for cooperation.”[55] As defence and technology partnerships diversify, India’s dependence on Russia may run its natural course and diminish. France demonstrates this approach by maintaining a strong, autonomous partnership with India despite differing positions on Russia.

The SoIA should be prioritised to unlock Indian participation, as a third country, in select Permanent Structured Cooperation (PESCO)[56] projects involving advanced capability development, and other EU security and defence initiatives. As Ambassador Delphin said in February, the SDP is the “political enabler” whereas the SoIA will be the “legislative enabler.”[57]

The EU-India Defence Industry Forum should act as a matchmaking hub, identifying specific platforms where Indian manufacturing and European R&D are complementary, encouraging joint ventures, and assessing the scope for co-production or sharing of military technologies.

Europe is increasingly open to third-country suppliers. Former EU foreign policy chief Josep Borrell urged member states to procure from third-country suppliers if it proved “better, cheaper, and quicker,”[58] and current foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, during her visit to New Delhi in January 2026, affirmed Europe’s intention to increasingly source defence capabilities from outside the bloc.[59] Joint projects can be structured to balance content requirements and provide access to SAFE.

An innovation-oriented partnership could become a pillar of India-EU security cooperation by promoting joint research, technology development, and collaboration between defence startups. Building on India's Innovations for Defence Excellence (iDEX) programme[60] and the India–US INDUS-X initiative,[61] New Delhi could consider joining the EU Defence Innovation Scheme (EUDIS)[62] to strengthen cooperation in emerging defence technologies. With more than 650 startups and over 10,000 MSMEs participating in defence projects,[63] iDEX has demonstrated the value of integrating innovation into military capability development. The European Defence Fund (EDF) supports collaborative defence research and innovation across member states, and has funded 224 European defence projects worth 4 billion euro since 2021.[64] Greater interaction between the iDEX and EDF ecosystems can facilitate knowledge exchange and encourage joint defence projects, while moving defence cooperation beyond government-to-government contracts.

The EU-India Trade and Technology Council (TTC)[65] can catalyse defence industrial cooperation. Many of its priority areas, including semiconductors, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, quantum technologies, telecommunications, space, and resilient supply chains, are inherently dual-use and critical to modern defence applications. By fostering trusted technology partnerships, regulatory convergence, innovation, and supply chains, the TTC can create the foundations for closer defence collaboration without directly addressing arms procurement.

Finally, India should reciprocate the EU’s 2023 appointment of a military attaché to New Delhi by posting one to Brussels. This would help sustain strategic dialogue and support growing defence-industrial ambitions on both sides.

The EU-India SDP reflects a recognition that the partnership need not rest on complete policy convergence. While differences persist, both sides share sufficient strategic alignment, complementary capabilities, and a common interest in navigating an increasingly contested geopolitical environment.[66] The challenge, therefore, is not to eliminate disagreements but to manage them through pragmatic, compartmentalised cooperation focused on tangible outcomes.

At the heart of the partnership is the shared pursuit of greater strategic autonomy. Defence industrial cooperation offers a tremendous opportunity to translate wider convergence into lasting strategic value. As a 2025 report by the Council for Strategic and Defense Research emphasised, “the structural conditions for a transformative partnership now exist in ways they have not previously.”[67] India’s expanding defence manufacturing base, combined with Europe’s advanced technological capabilities, creates a natural basis for collaboration amidst shifting defence dynamics. Meaningful industrial collaboration would deepen strategic trust and embed India and Europe more firmly within each other’s evolving security architectures. It would diversify defence supply chains, reduce strategic vulnerabilities, strengthen production capacity, and move the relationship beyond a traditional buyer-seller model towards long-term industrial interdependence.

SDPs are essentially statements of political willingness. The EU-India SDP does not itself establish a binding industrial arrangement. What it provides is the institutional and regulatory framework needed to convert political intent into concrete cooperation. Its success will depend on whether both sides move beyond declarations and implement joint defence projects. Otherwise, it risks following the trajectory of earlier initiatives, such as the EU-India Connectivity Partnership, launched in 2021,[68] whose implementation has remained limited.

Even though defence-industrial cooperation may continue to be driven by member states, the SDP reinforces and adds weight to these defence linkages by providing an overarching strategic framework and political messaging. If operationalised by pooling capabilities and resources, it could become a durable pillar of both Indo-Pacific and European security, helping shape the balance of power and serving as a stabilising force amidst intensifying geopolitical competition.
